analysis.one_liner: Lets workers win compensatory and punitive money damages for intentional job discrimination, and applies the same rights to congressional employees.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single Republican senator with no cosponsors, never left the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and died without a vote when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let workers who prove they were deliberately discriminated against because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or disability collect compensatory damages (for things like emotional distress) and, in cases of malice or reckless indifference, punitive damages on top of back pay. Awards would be capped depending on employer size, and either side could ask for a jury. It also extended the same rights to employees of the Senate, House, and congressional agencies, with enforcement handled inside each chamber rather than in court. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who can prove intentional workplace discrimination would gain a new route to money damages beyond lost wages, including compensation for emotional harm and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference. Either party could demand a jury trial, and prevailing parties could collect attorney's fees. Congressional and legislative-branch employees would gain formal coverage for the first time under these provisions.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal right to compensatory damages for future losses, emotional suffering, and mental anguish in intentional employment discrimination cases under Title VII and the ADA, plus punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference [S2][S3].
Sets dollar caps so both sides know the exposure: up to $50,000 for employers with 100 or fewer workers, $100,000 for employers with 101-500, and $300,000 for larger employers [S3].
Lets either party demand a jury trial when damages are sought, while barring the court from telling the jury about the caps [S2][S3].
Allows attorney's fees in actions enforcing the new damages provisions, which makes it feasible for individual workers to bring claims [S2][S3].

Extends the same rights and protections to employees of the Senate, House, and congressional agencies such as the GAO and CBO, though claims against Senate employers would be investigated and decided by the Senate Ethics Committee rather than a court [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers found to have intentionally discriminated would pay the compensatory and punitive damages, up to the caps, plus attorney's fees in enforcement actions. Employers defending disability accommodation claims could avoid damages by showing good-faith efforts to find a reasonable accommodation that would not cause undue hardship.

drawbacks.text: The caps limit recovery sharply: a worker discriminated against by a small employer could recover at most $50,000 in compensatory and punitive damages combined, regardless of the harm [S3].

Workers are excluded from the new damages if they can already recover under section 1981 (the Reconstruction-era civil rights statute), creating a two-track system where the remedy available depends on which statute the claim falls under [S2][S3].
Employers get a defense against damages in disability cases by showing good-faith accommodation efforts, which could blunt the remedy for workers whose requests were mishandled [S2][S3].

For Congress's own employees, enforcement would run through internal chamber bodies such as the Senate Ethics Committee, with exclusive jurisdiction inside the Senate, rather than through the federal courts available to private-sector workers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real, if modest, new remedy: money damages beyond back pay for workers who prove intentional discrimination, with jury trials and fee-shifting to make claims practical. The costs fall on employers who lose discrimination cases, and the caps keep awards predictable for both sides. The weakest part is Congress covering itself through internal committees instead of the courts, giving congressional employees a formal right but a weaker forum than private-sector workers would get.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. John Danforth introduced the bill on June 27, 1991, as Congress was working on legislation to expand remedies for workplace discrimination [S1][S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, where it stayed [S5].
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action appears in the record before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Under this bill's own record, employers escaped the specific damages liability and fee-shifting it would have imposed. Workers who face intentional discrimination went without the new remedies this bill offered, since nothing like it advanced from this bill.

for.name: Sen. John C. Danforth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 27, 1991; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action on it; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and the record shows no votes or partisan divisions on it.

industries.note: The bill would have created new financial exposure for employers found to have intentionally discriminated, with capped compensatory and punitive damages, jury trials, and attorney's fees. The bill's death means that exposure never took effect through this vehicle.
An attorney's fees provision would have let lawyers representing discrimination victims recover fees from losing employers, making small claims economically viable. The provision died with the bill.

industries.industry: Congress as an employer (Senate, House, and legislative-branch agencies)
industries.note: The bill would have applied the new anti-discrimination rights to congressional employees for the first time under these provisions, but enforcement would sit inside each chamber rather than in court. This bill never passed, so the coverage remained hypothetical.
